The stock barely moved today—up just 0.07%—as the refining sector faces crosscurrents. US oil prices fell to $101.91 per barrel over the past two days following hopes for Middle East diplomatic progress, which typically pressures refiner margins (the difference between what crude costs and what refined products sell for). That decline offset support from the escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which had spiked Brent crude to $109 earlier in the week and normally benefits refiners by tightening global supply.

Refineries are running at 93.5% capacity with healthy fuel inventories, leaving less room for volume growth to boost earnings. The week-long 7.5% rally through yesterday appears to have stalled as traders weigh whether diplomatic progress will stick—and how much refining demand a potential oil supply glut from Venezuelan crude (signaled by U.S. interest in India's Reliance) might create down the road.
